tagline: An island road linking a former port with colonial history
intro: The Roanoke Voyages Corridor is one of North Carolina’s scenic byways. Its island setting lies between the mainland and the barrier islands near Nags Head, with Croatan Sound to the west and Roanoke Sound to the east. U.S. 64 connects the mainland, Roanoke Island and the Outer Banks.

Plans for a mainland bridge began in the 1920s, but cost kept the State Highway Commission focused on primary highways. The crossing later named for William B. Umstead was built in 1955. In 2002, the Virginia Dare Memorial Bridge provided a more direct connection to the Washington Baum Bridge, allowing Outer Banks traffic to bypass Manteo.
John White’s settlers arrived on Roanoke Island in 1587. He returned to England for supplies, but war with Spain delayed his return until 1590; he found the settlement abandoned.

The older crossing leads from Manns Harbor over Croatan Sound to Roanoke Island. Fort Raleigh lies off U.S. 64 at the island’s north end, north of Manteo. Manteo holds Roanoke Island Festival Park; the Washington Baum Bridge connects Roanoke and Bodie islands farther along the road.

moments.title: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site
moments.text: Fort Raleigh preserves the location of the Roanoke Colony, where English settlement attempts took place in 1585 and 1587. The visitor-center museum also addresses a later colony: the island’s Freedmen’s Colony of 1863–1867. The Union Army established that settlement in 1863, allocating household plots and paying residents for Army work. The Freedmen’s Colony had more than 2,200 residents by 1864, with a sawmill, fisheries and 600 cabins. A marble monument erected in 2001 commemorates it. The site also houses the Waterside Theatre, where Paul Green’s outdoor drama The Lost Colony began in 1937.

moments.title: Manteo
moments.text: Manteo’s waterfront once linked the town by trade to Buffalo City, Edenton and Elizabeth City. Fishermen, boatbuilders and landowners put wealth into new development as the town grew into Dare County’s business center. It became the county seat in 1870 and incorporated in 1899. A road bridge to Nags Head changed the pattern of trade: downtown docks declined as commerce shifted toward the bridge road. The coastal warning display tower was restored in 2005. The town’s name honors Manteo, who traveled to London with the English in 1584 alongside Wanchese.

moments.title: Roanoke Island Festival Park
moments.text: The Elizabeth II is a modern representative of a sixteenth-century sailing vessel, with three masts, square rigging and a hull 69 feet long. Launched in 1983, the representative sixteenth-century ship became a State Historic Site in July 1984 during commemorations of the first English ships’ arrival four centuries earlier. The park’s museum carries the story beyond those voyages, with exhibits on maritime history, the Civil War and the local Freedmen’s Colony. A recreated American Indian settlement represents the period of the Roanoke Colony. The ship is seventeen feet wide and draws eight feet of water.
